claim: Human propensity to materiality consists in using, making, creating, and passing on technologies.
source: Our propensity to materiality, which consists in using, making, creating, and passing on technologies, has enabled us to shape the physical world according to our ends.
evidence: This is a definitional statement in the abstract that establishes what materiality means in the context of the study.

claim: Human propensity to materiality has enabled humans to shape the physical world according to their ends.
source: Our propensity to materiality, which consists in using, making, creating, and passing on technologies, has enabled us to shape the physical world according to our ends.
evidence: This is a general claim about human capability supported by established understanding of human technological development.

claim: Scientists have focused on either low-level skills such as motor cognition or high-level skills such as language or social cognition to explain human materiality.
source: To explain this proclivity, scientists have calibrated their lens to either low-level skills such as motor cognition or high-level skills such as language or social cognition.
evidence: This characterizes the existing scientific approach to studying materiality, representing a summary of the literature.

claim: Little has been said about the intermediate-level cognitive processes directly involved in mastering materiality, that is, technical cognition.
source: Yet, little has been said about the intermediate-level cognitive processes that are directly involved in mastering this materiality, that is, technical cognition.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study aims to address.

claim: A technical-reasoning process might be specifically at work in physical problem-solving situations.
source: Here, we show that a technical-reasoning process might be specifically at work in physical problem-solving situations.
evidence: This is a primary finding claim supported by the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The area PF within the left parietal lobe is central for technical reasoning in both tool-use and non-tool-use physical problem-solving.
source: We found via two distinct neuroimaging studies that the area PF (parietal F) within the left parietal lobe is central for this reasoning process in both tool-use and non-tool-use physical problem-solving and can work along with social-cognitive skills to resolve day-to-day interactions that combine social and physical constraints.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the neuroimaging data from both experiments.

claim: The area PF can work along with social-cognitive skills to resolve day-to-day interactions that combine social and physical constraints.
source: We found via two distinct neuroimaging studies that the area PF (parietal F) within the left parietal lobe is central for this reasoning process in both tool-use and non-tool-use physical problem-solving and can work along with social-cognitive skills to resolve day-to-day interactions that combine social and physical constraints.
evidence: This is supported by the mentalizing task data showing activation of both technical reasoning and mentalizing networks.

claim: There exists a specific cognitive module in the human brain dedicated to materiality.
source: Our results demonstrate the existence of a specific cognitive module in the human brain dedicated to materiality, which might be the supporting pillar allowing the accumulation of technical knowledge over generations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neuroimaging findings showing consistent activation of the left area PF across physical reasoning tasks.

claim: The cognitive module dedicated to materiality might be the supporting pillar allowing the accumulation of technical knowledge over generations.
source: Our results demonstrate the existence of a specific cognitive module in the human brain dedicated to materiality, which might be the supporting pillar allowing the accumulation of technical knowledge over generations.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the evolutionary and cultural significance of the findings.

claim: Modern societies heavily rely on and depend upon technology.
source: Modern societies heavily rely on and even depend upon technology.
evidence: This is a general statement about contemporary human society based on common knowledge.

claim: Technologies enable humans to fulfill elementary needs such as feeding or building shelters.
source: From the first lithic industries to the most modern and complex ones, technologies enable us to fulfil elementary needs such as feeding or building shelters, and even more sophisticated ones such as communicating, conquering space, or playing music.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the role of technology in human life.

claim: Technologies enable humans to fulfill sophisticated needs such as communicating, conquering space, or playing music.
source: From the first lithic industries to the most modern and complex ones, technologies enable us to fulfil elementary needs such as feeding or building shelters, and even more sophisticated ones such as communicating, conquering space, or playing music.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the role of technology in human life.

claim: Humans as a species are remarkably skilled at shaping the physical world according to their needs.
source: Human technology is ubiquitous and this omnipresence reflects how we, as a species, are remarkably skilled at shaping the physical world according to our needs (Boyd et al., 2011; Lombard, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyd et al., 2011 and Lombard, 2016.

claim: Only a little attention has been paid to the cognition needed to practically develop the technology required.
source: Even if this special skill has allowed our prolific expansion, only a little attention has been paid to the cognition needed to practically develop the technology required (Whiten, 2011; Wynn et al., 2017; Wynn and Coolidge, 2014; Whiten, 2022; van Elk, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations indicating a gap in the literature.

claim: Most understanding of neurocognitive processes involved in technology has come from clinical neuropsychology through observation of apraxic patients.
source: Most of this understanding has long come from clinical neuropsychology, through the observation of apraxic patients in whom damage to the left inferior part of the parietal lobe leads to tool-use disorders (De Renzi and Lucchelli, 1988; Goldenberg and Hagmann, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuropsychological studies.

claim: Damage to the left inferior part of the parietal lobe leads to tool-use disorders in apraxic patients.
source: Most of this understanding has long come from clinical neuropsychology, through the observation of apraxic patients in whom damage to the left inferior part of the parietal lobe leads to tool-use disorders (De Renzi and Lucchelli, 1988; Goldenberg and Hagmann, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Renzi and Lucchelli, 1988 and Goldenberg and Hagmann, 1998.

claim: Tool-use disorders have been initially interpreted as reflecting impaired sensorimotor programs dictating the prototypical manipulation of common tools.
source: These disorders have been initially interpreted as reflecting impaired sensorimotor programs dictating the prototypical manipulation of common tools (e.g., a hammer) (van Elk et al., 2014; Heilman et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Elk et al., 2014 and Heilman et al., 1982.

claim: The manipulation-based approach has provided interesting insights.
source: This manipulation-based approach has provided interesting insights (Kleineberg et al., 2022; Weiss et al., 2016; Kroliczak et al., 2021; Michalowski et al., 2022; Wheaton et al., 2009) and even elegant attempts to explain how these sensorimotor programs could support the use of both unfamiliar and novel tools (Buchmann and Randerath, 2017; Mizelle and Wheaton, 2010; Stoll et al., 2022; Seidel et al., 2023), but remains silent on the more general cognitive mechanisms behind human technology that include the use of common and unfamiliar or novel tools but must also encompass tool making, construction behaviour, technical innovations, and transmission of technical content.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies using the manipulation-based approach.

claim: The manipulation-based approach remains silent on the more general cognitive mechanisms behind human technology.
source: This manipulation-based approach has provided interesting insights (Kleineberg et al., 2022; Weiss et al., 2016; Kroliczak et al., 2021; Michalowski et al., 2022; Wheaton et al., 2009) and even elegant attempts to explain how these sensorimotor programs could support the use of both unfamiliar and novel tools (Buchmann and Randerath, 2017; Mizelle and Wheaton, 2010; Stoll et al., 2022; Seidel et al., 2023), but remains silent on the more general cognitive mechanisms behind human technology that include the use of common and unfamiliar or novel tools but must also encompass tool making, construction behaviour, technical innovations, and transmission of technical content.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of the manipulation-based approach as described in the literature.

claim: There is a behavioural link in left brain-damaged patients between common tool use and the ability to solve mechanical problems by using and even sometimes making novel tools.
source: This silence has been initially broken by a series of studies initiated by Goldenberg and Hagmann, 1998, which has documented a behavioural link in left brain-damaged patients between common tool use and the ability to solve mechanical problems by using and even sometimes making novel tools (e.g., extracting a target out from a box by bending a wire to create a hook) (Goldenberg and Hagmann, 1998; Heilman et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldenberg and Hagmann, 1998 and Heilman et al., 1997.

claim: Both common and novel tool uses are impaired after damage to the left inferior parietal lobe and particularly the area PF.
source: Brain-lesion studies have revealed that this behavioural link has a neural reality because both common and novel tool uses are impaired after damage to the left inferior parietal lobe and particularly the area PF (Goldenberg and Spatt, 2009; Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to brain-lesion studies by Goldenberg and Spatt, 2009 and Martin et al., 2016.

claim: The parietal lobe contribution to tool use concerns general principles of tool use rather than knowledge of the prototypical use of common tools and objects.
source: As (Goldenberg and Spatt, 2009) claimed, '[t]hese results support the conclusions that the parietal lobe contribution to tool use concerns general principles of tool use rather than knowledge of the prototypical use of common tools and objects, and the comprehension of mechanical interactions of the tool with other tools, recipients or materials rather than the selection of grip formation and manual movements' (p. 1653).
evidence: This is a direct quote from Goldenberg and Spatt, 2009.

claim: The parietal lobe contribution to tool use concerns the comprehension of mechanical interactions of the tool with other tools, recipients or materials rather than the selection of grip formation and manual movements.
source: As (Goldenberg and Spatt, 2009) claimed, '[t]hese results support the conclusions that the parietal lobe contribution to tool use concerns general principles of tool use rather than knowledge of the prototypical use of common tools and objects, and the comprehension of mechanical interactions of the tool with other tools, recipients or materials rather than the selection of grip formation and manual movements' (p. 1653).
evidence: This is a direct quote from Goldenberg and Spatt, 2009.

claim: The left area PF is preferentially activated when people observe others use tools.
source: For instance, evidence has indicated the preferential activation of the left area PF when people observe others use tools (Reynaud et al., 2019) as well as when people view physical events, whether they are instructed or not to reason about them (Fischer et al., 2016; Pramod et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reynaud et al., 2019.

claim: The left area PF is preferentially activated when people view physical events, whether they are instructed or not to reason about them.
source: For instance, evidence has indicated the preferential activation of the left area PF when people observe others use tools (Reynaud et al., 2019) as well as when people view physical events, whether they are instructed or not to reason about them (Fischer et al., 2016; Pramod et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2016 and Pramod et al., 2022.

claim: The cortical thickness of the left area PF predicts performance on psychotechnical tests.
source: Also, the cortical thickness of the left area PF was found to predict the performance on psychotechnical tests (Federico et al., 2022) (e.g., water-pouring problems).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Federico et al., 2022.

claim: Studies on the left area PF have also reported the involvement of other areas, such as the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) or the lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC).
source: It is noteworthy that these studies have also reported the involvement of other areas, such as the left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) or the lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC).
evidence: This is based on the cited neuroimaging studies mentioned in the preceding text.

claim: Technical reasoning refers to the ability of reasoning about the physical properties of objects.
source: Technical reasoning refers to the ability of reasoning about the physical properties of objects and is nurtured by implicit mechanical knowledge acquired through interactions with objects.
evidence: This is a definitional statement from the technical-reasoning hypothesis.

claim: Technical reasoning is nurtured by implicit mechanical knowledge acquired through interactions with objects.
source: Technical reasoning refers to the ability of reasoning about the physical properties of objects and is nurtured by implicit mechanical knowledge acquired through interactions with objects.
evidence: This is part of the definition of technical reasoning from the technical-reasoning hypothesis.

claim: Technical reasoning is both causal (i.e., prediction of future events) and analogical (i.e., transfer from one situation to another).
source: It is both causal (i.e., prediction of future events) and analogical (i.e., transfer from one situation to another).
evidence: This characterizes the nature of technical reasoning according to the technical-reasoning hypothesis.

claim: To solve a physical problem, an agent can use prior knowledge about mechanical properties and physical laws that apply to the physical world, such as gravity and leverage.
source: To solve a physical problem, an agent can use prior knowledge about mechanical properties and physical laws that apply to the physical world, such as gravity and leverage.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of technical reasoning according to the hypothesis.

claim: The outcome of the technical-reasoning process is a simulation of the mechanical action to be performed.
source: The outcome of the technical-reasoning process is a simulation of the mechanical action to be performed, which then constrains, if the individual intends to act, their bodily actions through a kind of mechanical-to-motor action cascade, which will ultimately feedback onto the central representations of our body, space, and objects.
evidence: This describes the output of technical reasoning according to the hypothesis.

claim: The left area PF occupies a central place in the technical-reasoning network, along with additional brain areas such as the left IFG and LOTC.
source: As mentioned above, the left area PF occupies a central place in the technical-reasoning network, along with additional brain areas such as the left IFG and LOTC.
evidence: This is based on the neuroimaging evidence cited earlier in the introduction.

claim: Scores were higher in the experimental conditions than for the control conditions for all the tasks.
source: As shown, scores were higher in the experimental conditions than for the control conditions for all the tasks (all p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 2 and statistical analysis.

claim: The experimental conditions were more difficult than the control conditions.
source: In other words, the experimental conditions were more difficult than the control conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results showing lower scores in experimental conditions.

claim: Some participants performed at or below the chance level in the experimental conditions whereas none did so in the control conditions.
source: This difference in terms of difficulty can also be illustrated by the fact that some participants performed at or below the chance level in the experimental conditions whereas none did so in the control conditions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The mechanical problem-solving task engaged an almost all-left network of areas, comprising the left supramarginal gyrus within the inferior parietal lobe (including the area PF), the left IFG (opercular and triangular parts), and the left superior parietal cortex and dorsal premotor cortex.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, the whole-brain analyses revealed that the mechanical problem-solving task engaged an almost all-left network of areas, comprising the left supramarginal gyrus within the inferior parietal lobe (including the area PF), the left IFG (opercular and triangular parts), and the left superior parietal cortex and dorsal premotor cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain fMRI analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The psychotechnical task generated a more bilateral network, with greater activation in both supramarginal gyri (including the left area PF but not the right area PF), the opercular part of both IFG, both LOTC, and both superior parietal and dorsal premotor cortices.
source: The psychotechnical task of Experiment 2 generated a more bilateral network, with greater activation in both supramarginal gyri (including the left area PF but not the right area PF), the opercular part of both IFG, both LOTC, and both superior parietal and dorsal premotor cortices (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain fMRI analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The whole-brain analyses indicated preferential activation in the left supramarginal gyrus (including the left area PF) in both the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task.
source: The whole-brain analyses indicated preferential activation in the left supramarginal gyrus (including the left area PF) in both conditions (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain fMRI analysis results shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The conjunction analysis of the four experimental conditions led to the only activation in the left supramarginal gyrus (including the left area PF).
source: Finally, the conjunction analysis of the four experimental conditions (the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task) led to the only activation in the left supramarginal gyrus (including the left area PF; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the conjunction analysis results shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The left area PF, central to the technical-reasoning network, is recruited in any situation requiring physical understanding.
source: These findings confirmed that the left area PF, central to the technical-reasoning network, is recruited in any situation requiring physical understanding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conjunction analysis and whole-brain results.

claim: The fluid-cognition task activated both dorsal prefrontal cortices and medial superior frontal cortices.
source: The whole-brain results for the fluid-cognition task of Experiment 2 confirmed our prediction (Figure 3C). We found activation of both dorsal prefrontal cortices and medial superior frontal cortices, which are characteristic to fluid cognition but not to technical reasoning.
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain fMRI analysis results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No activation of the inferior parietal lobes was found in the fluid-cognition task.
source: No activation of the inferior parietal lobes was found.
evidence: This is based on the whole-brain analysis of the fluid-cognition task.

claim: The PHYS-Only condition of the mentalizing task revealed a bilateral network of areas, comprising both supramarginal gyri (including the right area PF and the left area PF) and LOTC.
source: Concerning the mentalizing task of Experiment 2, the PHYS-Only condition revealed a bilateral network of areas, comprising both supramarginal gyri (including the right area PF and the left area PF as described above) and LOTC (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain fMRI analysis results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The INT + PHYS condition of the mentalizing task highlighted a bilateral network of areas comprising the left supramarginal gyrus (including the left area PF), both LOTC, the right IFG (opercular and triangular parts), both temporoparietal junctions (including the angular gyri) and the right temporal pole.
source: The INT + PHYS condition highlighted a bilateral network of areas comprising the left supramarginal gyrus (including the left area PF as described above), both LOTC, the right IFG (opercular and triangular parts), both temporoparietal junctions (including the angular gyri) and the right temporal pole (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain fMRI analysis results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The contrast of the INT + PHYS condition to the PHYS-Only condition revealed a network of bilateral areas that characterize the mentalizing network, namely both temporoparietal junctions (including both angular gyri), both medial prefrontal cortices, and the right temporal pole.
source: Importantly, the contrast of the INT + PHYS condition to the PHYS-Only condition revealed a network of bilateral areas that characterize the mentalizing network, namely both temporoparietal junctions (including both angular gyri), both medial prefrontal cortices, and the right temporal pole (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the contrast analysis results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: No activation of brain areas of the technical-reasoning network survived the contrast of INT + PHYS to PHYS-Only.
source: No activation of brain areas of the technical-reasoning network survived this contrast.
evidence: This is based on the contrast analysis of the mentalizing task conditions.

claim: ROI analyses confirmed greater activation of the left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task (p < 0.001).
source: The analyses confirmed the results obtained with the whole-brain analyses by indicating a greater activation of the left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task (all p < 0.001), but not in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35).
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: ROI analyses confirmed greater activation of the left area PF in the psychotechnical task (p < 0.001).
source: The analyses confirmed the results obtained with the whole-brain analyses by indicating a greater activation of the left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task (all p < 0.001), but not in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35).
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: ROI analyses confirmed greater activation of the left area PF in the PHYS-Only condition of the mentalizing task (p < 0.001).
source: The analyses confirmed the results obtained with the whole-brain analyses by indicating a greater activation of the left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task (all p < 0.001), but not in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35).
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: ROI analyses confirmed greater activation of the left area PF in the INT + PHYS condition of the mentalizing task (p < 0.001).
source: The analyses confirmed the results obtained with the whole-brain analyses by indicating a greater activation of the left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task (all p < 0.001), but not in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35).
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: ROI analyses did not show greater activation of the left area PF in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35).
source: The analyses confirmed the results obtained with the whole-brain analyses by indicating a greater activation of the left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task (all p < 0.001), but not in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35).
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Significant correlations were found between all the tasks that were hypothesized as recruiting technical reasoning (the psychotechnical task and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task) (all p < 0.05).
source: As shown in Figure 5, we found significant correlations between all the tasks that were hypothesized as recruiting technical reasoning, that is, the psychotechnical task and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task (all p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant correlation was obtained between the psychotechnical task and the fluid-cognition task (p > 0.15).
source: By contrast, no significant correlation was obtained between these three tasks and the fluid-cognition task (all p > 0.15).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant correlation was obtained between the PHYS-Only condition of the mentalizing task and the fluid-cognition task (p > 0.15).
source: By contrast, no significant correlation was obtained between these three tasks and the fluid-cognition task (all p > 0.15).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant correlation was obtained between the INT + PHYS condition of the mentalizing task and the fluid-cognition task (p > 0.15).
source: By contrast, no significant correlation was obtained between these three tasks and the fluid-cognition task (all p > 0.15).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The peaks of the fluid-cognition task were located more anteriorly, in the left area PFt and the postcentral cortex, compared to the peaks of the other four tasks, which were more posterior, in the left area PF.
source: As can be seen, the peaks of the fluid-cognition task were located more anteriorly, in the left area PFt (Parietal Ft) and the postcentral cortex, compared to the peaks of the other four tasks, which were more posterior, in the left area PF.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial analysis of individual activation peaks shown in Figure 6.

claim: The y coordinates of the peaks of the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task were posterior to the y coordinates of the peaks of the fluid-cognition task (all p < 0.05).
source: Indeed, the y coordinates of the peaks of the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task were posterior to the y coordinates of the peaks of the fluid-cognition task (all p < 0.05), whereas no significant differences were reported between the four tasks (all p > 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of y coordinates shown in Figure 6.

claim: No significant differences in y coordinates were reported between the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task (all p > 0.05).
source: Indeed, the y coordinates of the peaks of the mechanical problem-solving task, the psychotechnical task and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task were posterior to the y coordinates of the peaks of the fluid-cognition task (all p < 0.05), whereas no significant differences were reported between the four tasks (all p > 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of y coordinates shown in Figure 6.

claim: Participants recruited the same part of the left area PF to perform tasks involving technical reasoning.
source: These findings speak against the adjacency interpretation by revealing that participants recruited the same part of the left area PF to perform tasks involving technical reasoning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial analysis results showing consistent localization across technical reasoning tasks.

claim: The left area PF is systematically recruited in any situations involving physical events.
source: The first key finding is that the left area PF, central to the technical-reasoning network, is systematically recruited in any situations involving physical events, confirming the generalizable dimension of technical reasoning.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the neuroimaging results across all tasks.

claim: The technical-reasoning network is not recruited in other non-verbal and/or causal reasoning forms.
source: The second key finding is that the technical-reasoning network is not recruited in other non-verbal and/or causal reasoning forms, confirming that it is a specific form of reasoning oriented towards the physical world.
evidence: This is based on the lack of left area PF activation in the fluid-cognition task and the distinct activation patterns.

claim: Technical reasoning is a specific form of reasoning oriented towards the physical world.
source: The second key finding is that the technical-reasoning network is not recruited in other non-verbal and/or causal reasoning forms, confirming that it is a specific form of reasoning oriented towards the physical world.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the specificity results showing distinct networks for technical reasoning versus fluid cognition.

claim: A factor analysis with varimax rotation corroborated the orthogonality of technical-reasoning and fluid-cognition tasks.
source: For instance, in a recent study (De Oliveira et al., 2019), the technical-reasoning skills and fluid-cognition skills of 245 participants were assessed with tasks close to those employed here for assessing these two forms of reasoning. A factor analysis with varimax rotation was conducted and corroborated the orthogonality of technical-reasoning and fluid-cognition tasks.
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Oliveira et al., 2019.

claim: Previous studies have indicated the key role of the prefrontal cortex in fluid cognition.
source: At the cerebral level, previous studies have indicated the key role of the prefrontal cortex in fluid cognition (Hobeika et al., 2016), which is also found in the present results.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hobeika et al., 2016 and confirmed by the present study's results.

claim: Technical reasoning is a non-verbal form of reasoning specific to the physical domain that must be distinguished from fluid cognition.
source: However, we did not report any engagement of the technical-reasoning network in the fluid-cognition task, confirming that technical reasoning is a non-verbal form of reasoning specific to the physical domain that must be distinguished from fluid cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the distinct neural networks found for technical reasoning and fluid cognition.

claim: Causal reasoning has distinct forms and recruits distinct networks of the human brain (Social domain: Mentalizing; Physical domain: Technical reasoning).
source: In broad terms, the results of the mentalizing task indicate that causal reasoning has distinct forms and that it recruits distinct networks of the human brain (Social domain: Mentalizing; Physical domain: Technical reasoning), which can nevertheless interact together to solve day-to-day problems in which several domains are involved, such as in the INT + PHYS condition of the mentalizing task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mentalizing task results showing distinct but interacting networks.

claim: The mentalizing and technical reasoning networks can interact together to solve day-to-day problems in which several domains are involved.
source: In broad terms, the results of the mentalizing task indicate that causal reasoning has distinct forms and that it recruits distinct networks of the human brain (Social domain: Mentalizing; Physical domain: Technical reasoning), which can nevertheless interact together to solve day-to-day problems in which several domains are involved, such as in the INT + PHYS condition of the mentalizing task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the INT + PHYS condition results showing activation of both networks.

claim: The left IFG has been repeatedly found in previous research on technical reasoning.
source: The first additional area to consider is the left IFG, particularly its opercular part. This area has been repeatedly found in previous research on technical reasoning.
evidence: This is based on the literature review and the current study's findings.

claim: Activation of left IFG was reported in the mechanical problem-solving task at coordinates (–50; 7; 20).
source: We reported activation of left IFG in the mechanical problem-solving task (–50; 7; 20) and the psychotechnical task (–50; 7; 27).
evidence: This is based on the whole-brain analysis results.

claim: Activation of left IFG was reported in the psychotechnical task at coordinates (–50; 7; 27).
source: We reported activation of left IFG in the mechanical problem-solving task (–50; 7; 20) and the psychotechnical task (–50; 7; 27).
evidence: This is based on the whole-brain analysis results.

claim: A plausible hypothesis is that the left IFG integrates the multiple constraints posed by the physical situation to set the ground for a correct reasoning process.
source: The functional role of the left IFG in the context of tool use has been previously discussed (Reynaud et al., 2019) and a plausible hypothesis is that the left IFG integrates the multiple constraints posed by the physical situation to set the ground for a correct reasoning process, such as it could be involved in syntactic language processing (for a somewhat similar view, see Buxbaum and Randerath, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the function of the left IFG based on previous literature.

claim: Language and tool use share syntactic processes in the basal ganglia of the brain.
source: It has already been shown that language and tool use share syntactic processes in the basal ganglia of the brain (Thibault et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thibault et al., 2021.

claim: The LOTC was found activated in three experimental conditions (psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task).
source: Another additional area that has been found in three experimental conditions (psychotechnical task, and the PHYS-Only and INT + PHYS conditions of the mentalizing task) was the LOTC.
evidence: This is based on the whole-brain analysis results.

claim: The activation of LOTC could be related to familiarity with the tools or objects shown.
source: These specific activations could be related to familiarity with the tools or objects shown (Vingerhoets, 2008; Lesourd et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Vingerhoets, 2008 and Lesourd et al., 2021.

claim: The activation of the LOTC might reflect the involvement of semantic processes.
source: Thus, the activation of the LOTC might reflect the involvement of semantic processes whose involvement would remain to understand.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the LOTC activation.

claim: The cortical thickness of the left area PF predicts technical-reasoning and visuospatial performance.
source: A recent morphometry study (Federico et al., 2022) showed that the cortical thickness of the left area PF predicts technical-reasoning and visuospatial performance, whereas the right area PF only predicts visuospatial performance, confirming the distinction between these two abilities (Mitko and Fischer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Federico et al., 2022.

claim: The cortical thickness of the right area PF only predicts visuospatial performance.
source: A recent morphometry study (Federico et al., 2022) showed that the cortical thickness of the left area PF predicts technical-reasoning and visuospatial performance, whereas the right area PF only predicts visuospatial performance, confirming the distinction between these two abilities (Mitko and Fischer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Federico et al., 2022.

claim: The right area PF is recruited along with the left area PF when the task makes high demands on both technical and visuospatial dimensions.
source: These findings suggest that the right area PF is recruited along with the left area PF when the task makes high demands on both technical and visuospatial dimensions, as in the PHYS-Only condition of the mentalizing task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the right area PF activation.

claim: The literature has documented the recruitment of the left area PF in many neuroimaging experiments in which there was no need to reason about physical events.
source: The first limitation concerns the fact that the literature has documented the recruitment of the left area PF in many neuroimaging experiments in which there was no need to reason about physical events (e.g., language tasks).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation based on the broader neuroimaging literature.

claim: Understanding that the left area PF is central to physical understanding can be viewed as a first essential step before discovering its fundamental function.
source: Thus, understanding that the left area PF is central to physical understanding can be viewed as a first essential step before discovering its fundamental function, as suggested by the functional polyhedral approach (Genon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a perspective on how to interpret the findings in light of the functional polyhedral approach.

claim: The left area PF is recruited even in situations in which participants do not have to process common manipulable tools.
source: Here, we show that the left area PF is recruited even in situations in which participants do not have to process common manipulable tools.
evidence: This is based on the psychotechnical task results showing activation without common tool manipulation.

claim: The left area PF is not central to tool manipulation but to physical understanding.
source: The fact that we found a common activation of the left area PF in such tasks as well as in the mechanical problem-solving task, in which participants could nevertheless simulate the motor actions of manipulating novel tools, indicates that this brain area is not central to tool manipulation but to physical understanding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings arguing against the manipulation-based approach.

claim: The left area PF is more involved in tasks that focus on the mechanical dimension of the tool-use action than its motor dimension.
source: We have already shown that the left area PF is more involved in tasks that focus on the mechanical dimension of the tool-use action (e.g., the mechanical interaction between a tool and an object) than its motor dimension (i.e., the interaction between the tool and the effector [e.g., Reynaud et al., 2019; Reynaud et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by Reynaud et al., 2019 and Reynaud et al., 2016.

claim: The improvement of technology over generations is accompanied by an increase in its understanding.
source: Support for these accounts comes from micro-society experiments, which have demonstrated that the improvement of technology over generations is accompanied by an increase in its understanding (Osiurak et al., 2021; Osiurak et al., 2022), or that learners' technical-reasoning skills are a good predictor of cumulative performance in such micro-societies (De Oliveira et al., 2019; Osiurak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to micro-society experiments.

claim: Learners' technical-reasoning skills are a good predictor of cumulative performance in micro-societies.
source: Support for these accounts comes from micro-society experiments, which have demonstrated that the improvement of technology over generations is accompanied by an increase in its understanding (Osiurak et al., 2021; Osiurak et al., 2022), or that learners' technical-reasoning skills are a good predictor of cumulative performance in such micro-societies (De Oliveira et al., 2019; Osiurak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Oliveira et al., 2019 and Osiurak et al., 2016.

claim: Thirty-four participants took part in Experiment 1.
source: Thirty-four participants (Mage = 24.21, SD = 4.04, range: 18–36; female gender: n = 20, male gender: n = 14) took part in Experiment 1 and 35 new participants (Mage = 24.31, SD = 5.37, range: 20–44; female gender: n = 23, male gender: n = 12) in Experiment 2.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study sample.

claim: Thirty-five new participants took part in Experiment 2.
source: Thirty-four participants (Mage = 24.21, SD = 4.04, range: 18–36; female gender: n = 20, male gender: n = 14) took part in Experiment 1 and 35 new participants (Mage = 24.31, SD = 5.37, range: 20–44; female gender: n = 23, male gender: n = 12) in Experiment 2.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study sample.

claim: All participants were right-handed.
source: All the participants were right-handed, had a normal or corrected-to-normal vision, provided informed consent, and reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant inclusion criteria.

claim: The study was approved by a French Ethics Committee (N°ID-RCB: 2018-A00734-51).
source: The study was in line with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by a French Ethics Committee (N°ID-RCB: 2018-A00734-51).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about ethical approval.

claim: No participants were excluded based on head motion criteria.
source: Inclusion in the final sample required that head motion during scanning did not exceed 0.5 mm displacement (i.e., framewise displacement) between consecutive volumes on 90% of volumes. No participants were excluded based on this criterion.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data quality control.

claim: In the mechanical problem-solving task, participants had to figure out how to move a small red cubic element trapped in a 3D glass box from its original location into a new target location.
source: Before the scanning session, the participants were informed that, in the experimental condition, five distinct tools could be used to solve the mechanical problems (Figure 1A), which consisted in moving a small red cubic element trapped in the 3D glass box from its original location into a new target location.
evidence: This describes the task design as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the psychotechnical task experimental condition, participants had to select which of the two presented situations was the correct one or the most effective one.
source: The participants had to select which of the two presented situations was the correct one or the most effective one in the experimental condition (Figure 1B), whereas, in the control condition, they had to select the situation containing a square (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the task design as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The fluid-cognition task experimental condition required fluid reasoning.
source: The experimental condition required fluid reasoning (Figure 1C) whereas the control condition required only visuospatial pattern completion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the task design as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the PHYS-Only condition of the mentalizing task, the selection only needed to understand the physical context.
source: For the two experimental conditions (i.e., INT + PHYS and PHYS-Only conditions; Figure 1D), the participants had to choose the cartoon with the probable ending to the story depicted in the three first drawings, and for the control condition, they had to select which cartoon was already present in the first three ones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). In the PHYS-Only condition, the selection only needed to understand the physical context.
evidence: This describes the task design as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the INT + PHYS condition of the mentalizing task, the selection needed to understand both the physical context and the social context.
source: In the INT + PHYS condition, the selection needed to understand both the physical context and the social context.
evidence: This describes the task design as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Neuroimaging data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma Scanner using a 64-channel head coil.
source: For both experiments, 'neuroimaging data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma Scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) using a 64-channel head coil.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data acquisition.

claim: Results maps were presented with a significance threshold set at p < 0.05 with family-wise error (FWE) correction at the cluster level.
source: We present results maps with a significance threshold set at p < 0.05 with family-wise error (FWE) correction at the cluster level unless stated otherwise.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about statistical thresholding.
